title: Forces and elasticity — stretching springs
examTip: Know F = ke by heart, with e in metres. Know that it only works up to the limit of proportionality. Be ready to read a force–extension graph and work out a spring constant from it.
introTips: To change the shape of a still object, you need more than one force. One force on its own would just make it move.
Elastic deformation goes back to its first shape. Inelastic deformation does not.
F = ke links force and extension. It only works up to the limit of proportionality.
intro: Springs, rubber bands and trampolines all change shape when you push or pull them. In this lesson you learn which forces change an object's shape. You learn how extension depends on force. You also learn how a stretched spring stores energy.

keyPoints.heading: Changing shape: stretching, bending and compressing
keyPoints.content: Forces can change the shape of an object. There are three ways to do this. - Stretching: two forces pull the ends apart. Example: pulling both ends of a spring. - Bending: forces push on a beam in different places. Example: a diving board bending under a diver. - Compressing: two forces push the ends together. Example: squashing a spring between your hands. For a still object, more than one force must act to change its shape. With only one force, the object would not stay still. It would move off in the direction of the force. Example: a spring hanging from a clamp. The masses hanging on it pull down, and the clamp pulls up. The two forces together stretch it. Elastic deformation: the object goes back to its first shape and length when the forces are removed. A spring that is not stretched too far does this. Inelastic deformation: the object does not go back to its first shape when the forces are removed. A spring stretched too far stays longer.
writeBullets: Forces can stretch, bend or compress an object
A still object needs more than one force to change shape
With one force only, the object would move instead
Elastic deformation: goes back to its first shape when forces are removed
Inelastic deformation: does not go back to its first shape

keyTerms.def: A change of shape where the object goes back to its first shape and length when the forces are removed
A change of shape where the object does not go back to its first shape when the forces are removed

keyPoints.memTip: Elastic = Every time it comes back. Inelastic = It never comes back.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Ask why one force cannot change the shape of a still object. The answer is that one force would make it move instead.

keyPoints.heading: Force and extension: F = ke
keyPoints.content: The extension of an elastic object, such as a spring, is how much longer it gets. Extension = stretched length − first length. The extension is directly proportional to the force applied. This is true as long as the limit of proportionality is not exceeded. Double the force, and the extension doubles. The equation is F = ke. - F is the force, in newtons (N). - k is the spring constant, in newtons per metre (N/m). - e is the extension, in metres (m). A stiff spring has a large spring constant. You need a big force to stretch it a little. The same equation works for compression. Then e is how much shorter the object gets. Worked example: a force of 4 N stretches a spring by 0.08 m. k = F ÷ e = 4 ÷ 0.08 = 50 N/m.
writeBullets: Extension = stretched length − first length
Extension is directly proportional to force, up to the limit of proportionality
F = ke: force (N) = spring constant (N/m) × extension (m)
Also works for compression: e is then the compression
Spring constant k = F ÷ e. A stiffer spring has a bigger k

keyTerms.def: How much longer an object gets when it is stretched, in metres
The force needed per metre of extension, in N/m; F = ke
The point after which extension is no longer directly proportional to force

keyPoints.memTip: F = ke: Force = k times extension. Always put e in metres.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Students often use the stretched length instead of the extension. Check they take away the first length.

keyPoints.heading: Investigating force and extension
keyPoints.content: In a required practical, you investigate how the extension of a spring depends on the force. Method: - Hang the spring from a clamp. Put a ruler next to it. - Measure the spring's first length. - Hang a mass on the spring. Measure the new length. - Work out the extension. Extension = new length − first length. - Add more masses one at a time. Measure the length each time. The force on the spring is the weight of the masses. Work it out with W = mg. Plot a graph of force against extension. Two shapes can appear. - A linear relationship gives a straight line through the origin. Force and extension are directly proportional. - A non-linear relationship gives a curve. This happens once the limit of proportionality is passed. On the straight part, the gradient of the force–extension graph is the spring constant.
writeBullets: Hang spring from a clamp with a ruler beside it; measure first length
Add masses one at a time; measure the length each time
Extension = new length − first length; force = weight of masses (W = mg)
Linear: straight line through the origin — force and extension directly proportional
Non-linear: curve — the limit of proportionality has been passed
Gradient of the straight part of a force–extension graph = spring constant

keyTerms.def: A straight-line graph through the origin; the two quantities are directly proportional
A curved graph; the two quantities are not directly proportional

keyPoints.memTip: Straight line through zero = proportional. Bend in the line = limit of proportionality passed.
keyPoints.tutor_note: If the student plots length instead of extension, the line will not go through the origin. Use this to check their graph.

keyPoints.heading: Work done and elastic potential energy
keyPoints.content: A force that stretches or compresses a spring does work. The energy is stored in the spring as elastic potential energy. If the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done on it equals the elastic potential energy stored. Up to the limit of proportionality, you can work out the energy stored with this equation. You are given it in the exam. Ee = ½ke² - Ee is the elastic potential energy, in joules (J). - k is the spring constant, in N/m. - e is the extension, in m. Worked example: a spring has k = 50 N/m. It is stretched by 0.08 m. Ee = 0.5 × 50 × 0.08² = 0.5 × 50 × 0.0064 = 0.16 J.
writeBullets: Stretching or compressing a spring does work on it
The energy is stored as elastic potential energy
Not inelastically deformed: work done = elastic potential energy stored
Ee = ½ke² (given in the exam). Only up to the limit of proportionality
e is squared: double the extension gives four times the energy

keyTerms.def: Energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object; Ee = ½ke²

keyPoints.memTip: Work in = energy stored, as long as the spring springs back.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Watch for students who forget to square the extension. Ask them to square e first, then multiply.

rows: elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × extension²

0.question: A spring is stretched and then let go. It goes back to its first length. What kind of deformation was this?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. The spring went back to its first length, so the deformation was elastic.
0.wrongFeedback: The spring went back to its first length when the force was removed. That is elastic deformation. Inelastic deformation is when the object stays changed.

1.question: A force of 6 N stretches a spring by 0.03 m. The limit of proportionality is not passed. What is the spring constant?
1.wrongFeedback: Rearrange F = ke to get k = F ÷ e. So k = 6 ÷ 0.03 = 200 N/m.

2.question: A student plots force against extension for a spring. The line is straight through the origin, then curves. What does the curve show?
options: The limit of proportionality has been passed
The masses were added in the wrong order
2.correctFeedback: Correct. Once the line curves, force and extension are no longer directly proportional. The limit of proportionality has been passed.
2.wrongFeedback: A straight line through the origin means force and extension are directly proportional. A curve means this has stopped. The limit of proportionality has been passed.

3.question: A spring with k = 100 N/m is stretched by 0.2 m. It is not inelastically deformed. How much elastic potential energy is stored?
3.wrongFeedback: Use Ee = ½ke². Square the extension first: 0.2² = 0.04. Then 0.5 × 100 × 0.04 = 2 J.

commonMistakes: Using the stretched length instead of the extension. Extension = stretched length − first length.
Leaving the extension in centimetres. Change it to metres before using F = ke or Ee = ½ke².
Using F = ke past the limit of proportionality. After that point, force and extension are not directly proportional.
Forgetting to square the extension in Ee = ½ke².
examTips: In spring calculations, write the equation first. Then put in the numbers with units.
When asked to describe the practical, say how you measure the extension. Say how you work out the force.
When a graph is straight through the origin, say force and extension are directly proportional.
revisionCardBullets: Changing the shape of a still object needs more than one force
Stretching, bending and compressing all change shape
Elastic deformation: goes back to first shape. Inelastic: does not
F = ke: force (N) = spring constant (N/m) × extension (m)
Extension is directly proportional to force up to the limit of proportionality
Force–extension graph: straight line through origin = linear; curve = non-linear
Gradient of the straight part = spring constant
Work done stretching a spring = elastic potential energy stored (if not inelastically deformed)
